943c6910da212752: Di Malaysia, apa sahaja bisa menjadi isu politik. Termasuklah bahasa, sebagaimana tindakan sesetengah netizen cuba mengapi dan mengasapkan pemulauan terhadap rantaian kedai kopi (kopitiam) Oriental Kopi dengan alasan pelayannya kurang mahir berbahasa Melayu, selain menunya tidak cermat kerana tiada di dalam bahasa kebangsaan.
Selamat datang ke politik berbahasa di Malaysia. Apakah dimensi politik bahasa ini? Bagaimanakah cultural authority sedia ada bermain peranan?

Ketika menyampaikan titah diraja pada Istiadat Pembukaan Penggal Kelima Majlis Parlimen ke-15 di Parlimen pada 19 Jan 2026, Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim bertitah sebarang usaha untuk mengadakan sistem pendidikan baharu mesti dibuat selari dengan dasar pendidikan kebangsaan. Satu hal yang menonjol pada ucapan baginda itu adalah penegasan agar bahasa Melayu menjadi bahasa utama kerana ia adalah bahasa kebangsaan. "Oleh itu, sebarang usul untuk mengiktiraf apa juga sistem pendidikan lain mesti menerima bahasa Melayu dan sejarah Malaysia".

Isu ini bukanlah sederhana, ia membawa kita kembali kepada persoalan kewarganegaraan di mana bukan Melayu yang bersedia menerima identiti Malaysia perlu menerima pula bahasa Melayu sebagai bahasa rasmi, mestilah boleh dan bersedia bertutur dalam bahasa tersebut. Titah Sultan Ibrahim tersebut tidak syak lagi merupakan singgungan mengenai isu berkait UEC (Sijil Peperiksaan Bersepadu).

UEC adalah peperiksaan berpusat yang dikendalikan oleh Sekolah Menengah Persendirian Cina (SMPC) di bawah Gabungan Persatuan Guru Sekolah Cina Malaysia (Jiao Zong). Ia bukanlah peperiksaan di bawah Kementerian Pendidikan dan tiada kaitan dengan Sekolah Jenis Kebangsaan Cina di bawah Kementerian Pendidikan. Kelemahan atau ketidakmampuan sebahagian besar pelajar berbangsa Cina menguasai bahasa Melayu bukanlah sesuatu yang terbina dari persepsi politik tetapi telah pun dibuktikan dalam pelbagai kajian akademik, antara lain oleh Ang Lay Hoon dan Che Radiah Mezah, menerusi makalah ilmiah 'Masalah Penggunaan Bahasa Melayu dalam Kalangan Pelajar Etnik Cina di Malaysia' pada tahun 2012.

Masyarakat Cina berusaha melobi parti-parti politik untuk mengiktiraf UEC. Mereka yang menyokong pengiktirafan UEC menegaskan ia adalah bahagian daripada hak asasi manusia, akses adil kepada pendidikan dan peluang kerjaya, dan sama sekali bukan satu ancaman kepada bahasa kebangsaan, iaitu bahasa Melayu. Isu ini ditunggang oleh ahli-ahli parti politik khusus dalam helah memomokkan kelompok masyarakat Cina yang dianggap gagal mengasimilasi kebudayaan kebangsaan. Manakala, kelompok kanan Melayu pula beranggapan ia sebagai satu ancaman dan sengaja mencabar Dasar Pendidikan Kebangsaan, di mana naratif yang diketengahkan adalah UEC tidak selari dengan Falsafah Pendidikan Kebangsaan memandangkan silibus sejarah dan bahasa pengantar di sekolah persendirian Cina ini menggunakan bahasa Mandarin.

Loke Siew Fook, setiausaha agung DAP, parti yang mendapat sokongan meluas pengundi berbangsa Cina berulang kali menyatakan bahawa sebahagian besar pelajar UEC menguasai bahasa Melayu dan mengambil peperiksaan Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) bagi memastikan kelayakan mereka menepati standard kebangsaan.

Untuk mengambil jalan tengah, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim menyatakan kerajaan tidak mengiktiraf sukatan pelajaran UEC secara rasmi, sebaliknya sekadar memberikan laluan bersyarat untuk kemasukan lulusan tertentu ke institusi pendidikan tinggi tempatan dengan syarat wajib lulus bahasa Melayu dan sejarah.

Bahasa Melayu adalah bahasa kebangsaan dan bahasa rasmi mengikut Perkara 152 Perlembagaan. Mana-mana pelajar UEC yang berhasrat memasuki universiti awam di Malaysia wajib memperoleh sekurang-kurangnya gred kepujian (kredit) dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu di peringkat SPM. Ini bagi memastikan mereka mempunyai kompetensi linguistik untuk berinteraksi dan berfungsi dalam ekosistem awam Malaysia.

Selain itu, pengetahuan tentang sejarah tanah air dianggap sebagai asas kepada pembentukan jati diri dan kesetiaan kepada negara. Oleh demikian lulus dalam mata pelajaran sejarah SPM dijadikan syarat wajib yang tidak boleh dikompromi. Ini bagi memastikan setiap mahasiswa di universiti awam, tanpa mengira latar belakang sekolah mereka, dapat berkongsi naratif sejarah watan yang sama.

Pada masa sama aktivis pendidikan yang objektif menggesa Persekutuan Persatuan Lembaga Pengurus Sekolah Cina Malaysia (Dong Zong) menunjukkan keterbukaan bagi membenarkan elemen-elemen sastera, geografi, dan sivik tempatan diintegrasikan ke dalam silibus mereka. Mereka berpandangan pengiktirafan bersifat dua hala; di mana pihak kerajaan juga berhak menuntut penyesuaian terhadap aspirasi nasional dan ia mesti dilaksanakan oleh pihak pengurusan UEC. Harapannya adalah menerusi pendekatan berhati-hati ini, kemasukan pelajar UEC ke universiti awam tidak menggugat Dasar Pendidikan Kebangsaan dan Dasar Kebudayaan Kebangsaan. Bahkan ia boleh bertindak sebagai instrumen integrasi sosial yang menarik mereka graduan Sekolah Persendirian Cina ke dalam arus perdana pembinaan negara.

Seruan Sultan Ibrahim di Dewan Rakyat adalah satu bentuk penegasan cultural authority. Sebagai seorang raja, ia bukanlah kali pertama baginda menekankan pandangan. Pada tahun 2015, baginda mengkritik sistem pendidikan yang menggunakan bahasa Melayu, Mandarin dan Tamil yang dianggapnya menghalang penguasaan bahasa Melayu. Kritikan ini diulang lagi ketika baginda sudah menjadi Agong, di mana baginda menyatakan kehairanan mengapa masih ada rakyat Malaysia tidak boleh berbahasa Melayu, sambil menggesa agar sistem pendidikan negara menjadikan sistem pendidikan sekolah di peringkat rendah hanya satu aliran.

Isu kemampuan menguasai bahasa kebangsaan ini sudah tentu menjadi bahan rangup untuk kumpulan kanan Melayu, di mana penegasan terhadap kebudayaan kebangsaan yang berteraskan bangsa Melayu dipasakkan kembali. Gepena, yang merupakan gabungan kumpulan penulis berbahasa Melayu misalnya pernah mengambil kesempatan dengan meminta aktivis pendidikan Cina tunduk kepada kebudayaan kebangsaan yang berteraskan bangsa dan bahasa Melayu.

Tokoh kanan, dan Timbalan Presiden Muafakat Nasional, Ridhuan Tee Abdullah misalnya mengambil peluang ketidakmampuan graduan sekolah-sekolah Cina persendirian dan keengganan mereka untuk meningkatkan jam pembelajaran bahasa Melayu di sekolah sebagai satu keingkaran, dan mengisyaratkan agar kerajaan menggunakan kuasa dan kekerasan untuk membolehkan bahasa Melayu menjadi keutamaan. Ridhuan juga sering mengkritik papan tanda jalan yang tidak menggunakan bahasa kebangsaan. Dalam satu insiden yang melucukan tetapi dapat menggambarkan bagaimana cultural authority sering dipertengkar dan dipolitikkan, Ridhuan meminta sepanduk Hungry Ghost Festival yang disambut oleh masyarakat Cina ditulis dalam bahasa Melayu.

Selain manipulasi isu bahasa Melayu dalam bidang pendidikan yang ditunggang kumpulan dan tokoh kanan demi menunjukkan kejaguhan masing-masing; bahasa Melayu juga dijadikan bahan politik, untuk tujuan sama. Sebagai contoh, pada tahun 2025, dalam satu skandal sukan yang menyebabkan tujuh pemain antarabangsa digantung Fifa selama 12 bulan kerana memalsukan dokumen berkait status warisan, PAS menggunakan skandal tersebut untuk menjadikan Menteri Dalam Negeri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail sebagai sasaran.

Kerajaan Malaysia mendakwa seramai 23 pemain bola sepak telah diberi taraf kewarganegaraan Malaysia melalui proses naturalisasi sejak tahun 2018, dan ini termasuklah tujuh pemain warisan tersebut. Semua kelulusan ini dibuat mengikut peruntukan undang-undang serta Perlembagaan. Menteri dalam negeri seterusnya berhujah yang setiap permohonan diproses mengikut Perkara 19 Perlembagaan dan Kaedah-kaedah Warganegara yang menetapkan tiga syarat utama iaitu pemohon mesti bermastautin di Malaysia, berkelakuan baik serta mempunyai pengetahuan mencukupi dalam bahasa Melayu. Jawatankuasa Tatatertib Persekutuan Bola Sepak Antarabangsa (Fifa) mengenakan hukuman terhadap Persatuan Bolasepak Malaysia (FAM) dan tujuh pemain ini kerana melanggar Artikel 22 Kod Tatatertib Fifa berkaitan pemalsuan dokumen. Antara pemain terlibat ialah Gabriel Felipe Arrocha, Facundo Tomás Garcés, Rodrigo Julián Holgado, Imanol Javier Machuca, João Vitor Brandão Figueiredo, Jon Irazábal Iraurgui dan Hector Alejandro Hevel Serrano.

Ketua Penerangan PAS Fadhli Shaari dalam usaha memanjangkan skandal ini, dan untuk memerangkap menteri dalam negeri mencabar agar satu video ringkas tujuh pemain naturalisasi berbahasa Melayu disiarkan, memandangkan pengetahuan asas tentang bahasa itu adalah antara syarat wajib memperolehi kewarganegaraan. Sudah tentu Fadhli tidaklah seorang yang naif dan jahil seputar latar belakang skandal ini. Netizen yang bukan ahli Dewan Rakyat malah boleh menghidu kejadian dan angkubah kejadian ini. Fadhli, hanya mahu bermain 'sepak persepsi' untuk menyulitkan hidup seorang menteri; ditakdirkan keadaan terbalik, dan jika Fadhli yang berada di posisi itu, beliau sendiri akan berdepan jerebu solusi yang serupa.

Kedudukan bahasa Melayu sebagai sebahagian jati diri budaya bangsa Melayu dengan itu tidaklah sederhana. Pemuda Umno sebagai contoh menjadikan komitmen untuk terus mempertahankan agama Islam, memartabatkan bangsa Melayu serta memelihara institusi raja Melayu sebagai teras perjuangan. Walaupun komitmen tersebut sebetulnya hanyalah umpan politik dan 'acah-acah Doraemon' sahaja. Dalam banyak keadaan termasuk kes kedudukan bahasa Melayu, kumpulan kanan Melayu dan parti-parti politik misalnya dapat berlindung di sebalik raja Melayu sebagai cultural authority dalam memaksakan agenda politik mereka.

Sudah nasib Oriental Kopi tersedut dalam politik bahasa ini. Mungkin dengan kontroversi dan ancaman boikot ini, rangkaian kopitiam itu akan memperbaiki pemasaran dan persembahannya. Akan tetapi, sementara itu berlaku, ya pilihan raya sudah mendekat, maka politik bahasa sebagai keropok rangup akan terus dikunyah-kunyahi.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
dadce3f3f746bd61: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 15 — The Ministry of Defence (MinDef) is strengthening its commitment to the welfare and future of Malaysian Armed Forces (MAF) personnel and veterans through the MyBakat Veteran initiative, which aims to benefit more than 15,000 people by 2030.

Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the initiative underscores MinDef’s new approach to ensuring that MAF personnel receive support not only during their service but are also better prepared to pursue a second career after retirement.
He said the ministry is placing greater emphasis on aligning military skills and experience with industry requirements to broaden job opportunities for MAF personnel and veterans.

“We are moving away from the ‘train first, find a job later’ approach towards directly matching personnel’s competencies with industry needs, relevant training and actual career opportunities,” he said.
He said this at the signing of a Note of Cooperation between MinDef and the Ministry of Human Resources to implement MyBakat Veteran here yesterday.

MinDef secretary-general Datuk Lokman Hakim Ali and HR Ministry secretary-general Datuk Azman Mohd Yusof signed the Note of Cooperation in the presence of Mohamed Khaled and Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan.
Also present was Chief of Defence Force General Tan Sri Malek Razak Sulaiman.

A memorandum of understanding (MoU) was also signed by MinDef, the Armed Forces Ex-Servicemen Affairs Corporation (PERHEBAT) and the Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) to facilitate the placement of PERHEBAT trainees and MAF veterans with companies under MEF for a six-month transition period before they are absorbed into permanent positions.
Mohamed Khaled said the initiative focuses on career preparation at least two years before retirement, noting that between 5,000 and 7,000 MAF personnel leave the service each year.

“The strategic collaboration also offers opportunities for military experience and expertise to be recognised as professional qualifications through the Malaysian Skills Certificate (SKM) and Malaysian Skills Diploma (DKM), subject to competency assessments and eligibility criteria.

“It also strengthens the roles of PERHEBAT and the Malaysian Armed Forces Veterans Affairs Department (JHEV), with support from TalentCorp and relevant agencies, in providing career transition training and access to job opportunities,” he said.
He said the collaboration highlights MinDef’s efforts to expand the support ecosystem for MAF personnel through a more structured, integrated approach that responds to labour market needs. — Bernama
70402e54476f5164: KUALA LUMPUR: The BYD Seal driver involved in a six-vehicle crash that killed a 5-year-old girl along Jalan Kuching on Saturday was brought to the court complex to face three charges.
The 24-year-old man, dressed in a green shirt and handcuffed, was escorted to the magistrate's court by traffic police.
He was arrested yesterday after being discharged from a private hospital, where he had received treatment for a concussion sustained in the crash.
He was detained at the Dang Wangi police headquarters lock-up.

He is expected to face charges under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987 for causing death by reckless or dangerous driving, Section 42(1) for reckless and dangerous driving, and Section 52(1) for failing to stop and report an accident.
The crash occurred at 3.44pm on Saturday, killing the girl and injuring her father and a motorcyclist.
Five cars and a motorcycle were involved in the collision.
Initial investigations found that traffic was moving slowly from the city centre towards Segambut when the BYD Seal allegedly rear-ended a Perodua Bezza driven by the girl's 30-year-old father.
The impact sent the Bezza, which also collided with a motorcycle, spinning into the right lane, where it struck three other vehicles: a Nissan Almera, a Toyota Alphard and a Perodua Myvi.
The girl, who was seated in the rear of the Bezza, suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the Kuala Lumpur Hospital.
Her father sustained injuries to his right hand, while the 33-year-old Yamaha 135LC motorcyclist suffered head injuries.
Police later located the BYD Seal driver at the private hospital.
3b8f413372d6ee47: GURUN: Fourteen suspects, including two minors, will be charged at the Gurun Court today over the death of a teenager whose body was found along Jalan Harvard here seven days ago.
The suspects, all locals aged between 16 and 24, are expected to be charged under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
The 18-year-old victim was found by members of the public by the roadside with injuries to his head and face.

At a previous press conference, Kedah police chief Datuk Adzli Abu Shah said the teenager had been confined for two days, tortured and had his hair cut with scissors after being accused of stealing a motorcycle.
He said the victim was also beaten with blunt objects until he died. His body was then dumped by the roadside at the location.
A post-mortem conducted on the same day found that the cause of death was head injuries sustained from blunt-force trauma.
8ffd80606ba0acb0: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 15 — For Malaysian actor Zul Ariffin, getting a scene right is worth the extra effort, even if it means doing take after take to deliver his best performance.

Speaking at a media session for his latest horror film, Pemuja Syaitan, yesterday, Zul admitted that watching himself on the big screen at film premieres sometimes leaves him wondering what he could have done differently.
Those experiences, he said, have made him more determined to give his all during filming, even if it means repeating a scene until he is satisfied with the result.
“During the filmmaking process, we have a limited amount of time.
“Let's say we shoot for 30 days, 25 days, or 45 days.
“That is the only time we have control over, especially when it comes to filming,” he said at TGV Suria KLCC yesterday.
“We are only involved in the shooting process.
“Once filming is over, we move on to post-production, and we have no control over it.
“The best thing is to give it our all and do whatever it takes.
“If you want more takes, we do more takes.
“We do not want to look back a year later and regret it, thinking, ‘We should have done it that way.’
“I have experienced that before, and even now, I still think about things I should have done differently.
“You end up regretting it when you are sitting alone at the premiere, watching the film after all that hard work.”
His commitment has not gone unnoticed by Pemuja Syaitan director Liyana Jasmay, who recalled how Zul was willing to keep going even after completing 10 takes of a scene.
“He is a performer, so he really does not mind.
“Even if it takes 20 takes, he does not mind.
“I love that spirit, and I really hope Zul’s spirit will go to everybody,” she said at the media session.

In Pemuja Syaitan, Zul plays Inspector Zul, who investigates a bloody tragedy involving a group of former classmates whose reunion takes a deadly turn after they uncover a time capsule containing long-buried secrets and betrayals.
The horror thriller marks Liyana's theatrical feature directorial debut after years of working as an actress and directing telefilms.
Shot over 23 days, the film also stars Elizabeth Tan, Nadhir Nasar, Aila Azizul, Selena Jasmay, Marsha Biddulph, Hakim Khan, Nat Aaliyah, Aida Amron, Ellyza Azizi and Dhabita Auji.
Pemuja Syaitan opens in cinemas nationwide today.
1c3a8a0cbef29d95: KOTA KINABALU, Oct 15 — The Coroner’s Court here today concluded hearing the testimonies of all 83 witnesses in the inquest into the death of Zara Qairina Mahathir, with Coroner Amir Shah Amir Hassan fixing Friday morning for further directions on submissions.

Amir Shah, before adjourning today’s proceedings, said no further deponents would be called on Friday, with the court sitting at 9 am for directions on submissions in the inquest into the death of Zara Qairina.
“On Friday, I will hear from the parties and decide on the directions for submissions,” he said.
The coroner said the grounds for the verdict would be delivered in Bahasa Malaysia to make the inquest findings easier to understand.
Zara Qairina died at Queen Elizabeth Hospital on July 17, 2025, a day after she was found unconscious near a drain at her school hostel in the early hours of July 16.
On Aug 13, 2025, the Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) announced that an inquest would be conducted into Zara Qairina’s death after reviewing the investigation report submitted by police.
On Aug 8, 2025, the AGC said that Zara Qairina’s remains would be exhumed to allow for a post-mortem examination.
The exhumation at the Tanjung Ubi Muslim Cemetery, Kampung Mesapol, Sipitang, was completed at 7.15 pm on Aug 9, 2025.
The inquest into the death of the Form One student commenced on Sept 13 last year. — Bernama

2de9f2e2038ee51f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 15 — Malaysian actor Zul Ariffin is preparing to sink his teeth into one of the most challenging roles of his career, portraying the legendary Raja Bersiong in Astro Shaw’s upcoming film Baling.

Astro Shaw announced on October 13 that Zul will play Yong, also known as Raja Bersiong, the mythical fanged king associated with the ancient kingdom of Kedah in Malay folklore and literature, including Hikayat Merong Mahawangsa.
The character is traditionally depicted as a tyrannical ruler.
Baling is the latest addition to the Astro Shaw Cinematic Universe (ASCU), a shared fictional universe connecting characters and stories from the studio’s local films and television series.

Speaking to Malay Mail at a media screening of Pemuja Syaitan at Suria KLCC yesterday, Zul said he was looking forward to the role despite the challenges of bringing such a legendary figure to the big screen.
“For me, I’m more focused on playing Raja Bersiong,” he said.
For Zul, part of the challenge lies in introducing the character to a younger generation who may be unfamiliar with the legend and its place in Malay folklore.

“Growing up, I don’t think many of us knew much about the character, so establishing him and introducing his story to a new generation, especially children today, will be a challenge for me and the whole team,” he said.
The actor added that the role would push him beyond the physical demands of the performance.
“But I’m excited. It is easily one of the most challenging roles I’ve taken on, not just physically but in every aspect,” he said.
Zul said the production team was already hard at work but declined to reveal further details, given the film’s recent announcement.
Directed by Anwari Ashraf, Baling will follow Yong, also known as Raja Bersiong, as he confronts his dark past and seeks redemption.
Zul is the only cast member announced so far.
The film is slated for release in 2027.
a871560de81a4495: KUALA LUMPUR: EGH International Bhd is banking on a RM313.5 million order book, improving margins and a stronger balance sheet to drive earnings growth as the interior fit-out specialist prepares to make its debut on the ACE Market.
Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd has assigned the company a fair value of 18 sen per share, based on a forecast price-to-earnings ratio of 12 times, citing its project pipeline and earnings prospects.
The research house forecasts EGH International to register core net earnings of RM12.3 million in the financial year ending March 2027 (FY27) and RM14.6 million in FY28.

The company's outstanding order book comprises 18 projects, equivalent to about 1.7 times its revenue in FY26, providing earnings visibility over the next two financial years, with the bulk expected to be billed in the remainder of FY27 and FY28.
Among its notable projects are the Park Hyatt Hotel at Merdeka 118, valued at RM210.7 million, and the Antara Genting development, worth RM143.2 million.

Its largest outstanding project is Armani Hallson KLCC, valued at RM118.9 million, accounting for about 38 per cent of the current order book. Work on the project is scheduled to commence in January 2027.
EGH International has more than 15 years of experience providing turnkey interior fit-out services, covering design, procurement, construction and installation.
The business contributed about 92.1 per cent of the group's FY26 revenue, with the balance coming from the sale of furniture, fittings and equipment (FF&E) and building materials.

Rakuten Trade said the company's ability to secure more large-scale, high-specification projects would be crucial to sustaining growth, while its planned post-listing debt reduction could improve its capacity to compete for new contracts.
Of the initial public offering (IPO) proceeds, RM14.4 million will be allocated to repay borrowings, strengthening its financial flexibility and tendering capacity.
Following the listing, net gearing is forecast to fall to 0.04 times from 2.42 times currently, giving the company greater balance-sheet headroom to pursue new projects and expand its operations.
Beyond its core fit-out operations, EGH International is investing in infrastructure to support larger projects and broaden its revenue streams.
The company plans to construct a five-storey industrial building spanning 130,000 sq ft in Puchong to house its new headquarters, warehouse and showroom.
The expanded facilities are expected to strengthen its ability to handle larger fit-out contracts while providing a platform for the growth of its business-to-consumer (B2C) retail business.
Operating under the IPO World business and Interior Premium Outlet brand, the company sells FF&E products and building materials directly to consumers.
The segment has gained traction, with B2C sales increasing from RM1.1 million in FY23 to RM5.7 million in FY26.
To build on this growth, EGH International plans to establish a 25,000 sq ft flagship showroom at its new headquarters and open additional showrooms.
It is also developing a partner-based model that would enable interior designers and contractors to access artificial intelligence-powered design software linked to the company's product catalogue.

The initiative could create a new sales channel by connecting interior design work with product sourcing. However, with the model still at an early stage, the retail business is unlikely to be a significant near-term earnings driver.
EGH International's expansion plans come amid an expected increase in demand for interior fit-out services in Malaysia.

Independent market researcher Infobusiness Market Research Sdn Bhd projects the market to grow from RM4.7 billion in 2025 to RM6.1 billion in 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of 5.2 per cent.
The projected growth is underpinned by property market activity, an expanding hotel supply and rising demand from the private healthcare sector.
These segments offer opportunities for fit-out specialists as developers, hotel operators and healthcare providers require specialised interior construction and installation services.
For EGH International, the key challenge will be converting industry demand into new contracts while maintaining project execution and profitability.

Although its existing order book provides near-term revenue visibility, its ability to replenish that pipeline, improve margins and secure larger contracts will determine whether it can sustain earnings growth beyond FY28.
Its retail and technology initiatives offer additional avenues for expansion, but their contribution will depend on execution as the group scales up its facilities and broadens its customer reach.

e93c9d07611b0fcf: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 15 — The government is developing a sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) cloud to ensure the country’s classified information remains secure and beyond the reach of foreign laws and policies, said Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil.

He said the initiative was crucial to protecting Malaysia’s digital sovereignty, particularly in securing sensitive government information, including official documents, that could be at risk if stored on public cloud services.
“Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim previously mentioned this initiative, which we are now in the process of implementing. It is vital for our digital sovereignty, which is the sovereign cloud.

“We have observed that some countries have policies and laws that could make the use of public clouds less secure, especially when it comes to classified information. Therefore, the government has decided to develop a sovereign AI cloud,” he said.
Fahmi was speaking as a guest on Bernama TV Ruang Bicara programme, titled “Budget 2027: Empowering Communication, Driving the Orange Economy”, here yesterday.
He said the initiative would be managed by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) and the Communications Ministry.

Meanwhile, Fahmi said providing wider, faster, more affordable and secure Internet access was crucial to strengthening the country’s digital economy, which is estimated to contribute more than 25.5 per cent to gross domestic product (GDP).

He said Phase One of the National Digital Network (JENDELA) initiative had helped bridge the Internet access gap between urban and rural areas. However, connectivity challenges remained, particularly when users travelled beyond village areas.
“The issue arises when someone leaves a village and suddenly loses the signal. We need to ensure that connectivity remains uninterrupted,” he said.

He added that improved Internet connectivity would benefit entrepreneurs selling products online, students participating in digital learning, and members of the public accessing information or applying for government services online.
Fahmi said 5G technology could also improve efficiency in the agricultural sector through the use of the Internet of Things (IoT) and robotics.
Under Budget 2027, the government has allocated RM5 billion for JENDELA to expand high-quality Internet coverage, particularly in rural and remote areas. — Bernama
c5e41fa43619d78a: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 15 — The ringgit opened lower against the US dollar today as stronger-than-expected US inflation data bolstered expectations of a possible interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve (Fed), lending support to the greenback.
At 8 am, the ringgit edged down to 4.0820/0865 against the US dollar from yesterday’s close of 4.0805/0850.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the US Dollar Index (DXY) rose 0.36 per cent to 102.55 points after headline inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent in September from 3.4 per cent in August, exceeding the market consensus of 3.6 per cent.
He said core inflation also increased to 2.6 per cent in September from 2.4 per cent in August, surpassing the consensus estimate of 2.4 per cent.
Higher gasoline prices were the main driver, with the transport sub-index rising to 7.9 per cent in September from 6.2 per cent in August.

“Following the inflation data, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee described the figures as discouraging, suggesting that Fed officials should consider raising the federal funds rate at their upcoming meeting on Oct 27-28,” he told Bernama.
Mohd Afzanizam said the latest developments had strengthened expectations of a US rate hike, potentially putting further pressure on the ringgit.
“As such, we expect the US dollar-ringgit pair to trade within the RM4.08 to RM4.09 range today as expectations of a US rate increase gain momentum,” he said.

“Such a growth trajectory could support a possible normalisation of the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at some point in the future,” he added.
At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly lower against major currencies.

It strengthened against the British pound to 5.4005/4064 from 5.4132/4192 at Wednesday’s close, but weakened against the Japanese yen to 2.5840/5870 from 2.5751/5781. It also edged lower against the euro to 4.5694/5744 from 4.5673/5723.
Against its ASEAN peers, the ringgit traded mostly higher.

The local currency edged up against the Singapore dollar to 3.1794/1831 from 3.1829/1867 at Wednesday’s close and strengthened against the Thai baht to 12.1365/1586 from 12.1498/1672. It also rose against the Philippine peso to 6.49/6.50 from 6.50/6.51.

31cb74b33cd4cb65: JERUSALEM, Oct 15 — Israel’s army chief said yesterday that the military was reinforcing troop levels “across all fronts”, citing an increased risk of escalation as the country heads into elections this later month.

346cd0002971c260: KUALA LUMPUR: United Malacca Bhd's conditional mandatory general offer (MGO) at RM6.10 per share undervalues its plantation landbank and potential asset monetisation opportunities.

"This values the company at just 8.8 times its historical financial year 2026 price-to-earnings ratio and 0.81 times its price-to-net asset value.
"The offer also implies an enterprise value of RM33,449 per hectare," she said in a note.

The MGO was triggered after Prosper Trading Sdn Bhd acquired Great Eastern Life Assurance (Malaysia) Bhd's 13.44 per cent stake in United Malacca for RM171.9 million, raising the offerors' combined shareholding to 47.66 per cent.
Ng said the offerors also intend to settle an outstanding MGO obligation dating back to September 2024 through the current offer and a cash compensation scheme.
She said the offer price did not fully reflect the potential value of United Malacca's estates in Melaka, Negri Sembilan and Segamat, Johor, spanning a combined 2,834 hectares.
The estates have a net book value of RM188.1 million, equivalent to just 62 sen per square foot.
"United Malacca's net cash position of RM312.8 million, or RM1.59 per share, provides further support to its balance sheet," she said.
While the MGO provides a near-term exit opportunity, Ng said the offerors' intention to retain United Malacca's listing would allow investors to benefit from potential future land monetisation.
CIMB Securities maintained its "Buy" call on the stock with an unchanged target price of RM6.93, representing a 13.6 per cent upside from the offer price.
234ba1f3ae1065da: KYIV, Oct 15 — Ukraine yesterday accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem,” Zelensky told UK journalist Piers Morgan. “I don’t know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on.”
Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov later said that “Starlink’s operation at speeds up to 160 km/h is being restored. Strike drones and interceptor drones should be able to fly again”.
Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.

He drew a distinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to US President Donald Trump.
Zelensky replied in the affirmative when asked if he felt “betrayed” after Trump announced a diesel-supply deal with heavily sanctioned Moscow.

“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side. This is not (the) right side of history,”

Zelensky had framed the lack of warnings from allies about a wave of powerful strikes on Tuesday night and early Wednesday as “completely unjust”, and accused Russia of wilfully flouting a supposed “energy ceasefire” announced unilaterally by Trump.

A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks. Trump denied doing so on Tuesday.
Defence officials also suggested Washington was behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals which help Ukraine’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
“It’s obvious they (the United States) are helping Russia for some reason,” the senior official told AFP.
Zelensky adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov said the attacks and Starlink restrictions were more than a coincidence.
“Through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend the country against jet-powered Shahed drones,” he wrote on Telegram.
Close contact
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia was watching for any sign that Washington’s backing for Ukraine may have shifted.
“We are carefully noting all this. It is too early to draw any systemic conclusions,” he told reporters.
President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy on economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile said the first contracts on providing diesel to the United States would be signed in the coming days.
“We are in close, hourly contact with the American side, and everything is moving very quickly,” he added.
Trump, facing crunch mid-term elections next month, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on fuel supplies and increase in prices at the pump.
But most experts say the real reason is the joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran since late February, which have seen Tehran block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
‘Disrespect’

Ballistic missiles have now struck the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, for two nights running, before air raid sirens could sound in time to warn people to take cover in basements, bomb shelters or metro stations.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelensky, accusing Moscow of squandering a chance to ease hostilities.

The lack of warning has been reported only rarely during the conflict and Ukrainian officials have previously suggested the Russian military’s use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues could be to blame.
Fifteen people were killed around the country in the latest round of strikes, while significant damage to energy facilities and equipment knocked out power to swathes of Kyiv.
Power plants came under ballistic-missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, while Zhytomyr in the northwest, Sumy in the northeast and Chernigiv in the north were also hit.
Russia has previously targeted Ukraine’s power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20C. — AFP

49e1edf1c0eac735: LONDON, Oct 15 — Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the activist group Palestine Action, her publisher Faber said yesterday.

“Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said in a statement on its website.

“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence,” Rooney said in a statement shared with AFP.

bd0de512ee422ba3: OCTOBER 15 — Every day, Malaysians throw away about 39,000 tonnes of solid waste, more than our landfills can comfortably absorb. In 2024, the country generated 15.2 million tonnes of solid waste, and that figure is expected to climb to 17.03 million tonnes by 2035. At this rate, our landfills could reach full capacity by 2041. Much of this waste never needed to be buried. SWCorp estimates that nearly 40 per cent of what Malaysians send to landfill has recycling potential. Food waste alone makes up 44.5 per cent of household waste, and instead of being composted, it rots in landfills.

To deal with the pile-up, the government has turned to waste-to-energy (WtE) incinerators. The Jeram plant in Kuala Selangor, for example, can process up to 1,700 tonnes of waste a day and generate 26MW of electricity. But burning waste is only one option, and it should not be the first one.

Modern incinerators are far cleaner than older ones. That said, it’s important to note that their safety depends on careful operation. Operators must keep temperatures above 850°C to break down toxic dioxins and furans, and this must be maintained every day for the life of the plant. It is no surprise that residents near proposed sites, such as Rawang, have raised concerns about safety, health, the environment and traffic.

Waste-to-resource approaches carry far less risk. Composting food scraps, sorting paper or turning palm residue into fertiliser does not involve a smokestack. However, they do depend on one basic procedure: separating waste at source. Mixed, wet rubbish is difficult to recycle and difficult to burn. Even at Jeram, household waste must be dried for seven days before it can be incinerated. The government’s decision to make recycling facilities compulsory at shopping malls is a step in the right direction, and the same thinking should be applied to housing areas, wet markets and food courts.
The author argues that Malaysia should treat waste as a resource first, prioritising recycling, composting and recovery before resorting to waste-to-energy incineration. — Picture via Twitter/Bernama

The good news is that Malaysia already has a working recycling industry. In 2024, around 2.04 million tonnes of plastic, 1.77 million tonnes of metal and 1.49 million tonnes of paper were collected for recycling.

The bigger opportunity lies in agriculture. Malaysia produces roughly 60 million tonnes of biomass each year, much of it from the palm oil industry. Using fronds, trunks and empty fruit bunches as mulch has been estimated to save plantations up to RM450 per hectare a year in fertiliser costs. Smaller businesses cannot afford processing plants on their own, but they can share facilities through cooperatives, industry associations and universities.

The financial case is just as clear. Incinerators are expensive to build. The proposed Broga incinerator, for instance, was estimated to cost RM1.5 billion for a capacity of 1,500 tonnes a day. Once built, an incinerator needs a steady supply of waste to pay off its debt, which works against efforts to reduce and recycle. Recovered materials, on the other hand, can be sold. A manufacturer losing 5 per cent of RM500,000 worth of raw materials could save RM12,500 a year simply by halving that loss, without making a single extra sale.
As Malaysia moves towards a circular economy, the question is not whether we need waste-to-energy plants; it’s whether we can afford to burn materials that still have value.

Incineration has a role, but only for residual waste that cannot be reused. Malaysia’s recycling rate reached 37.9 per cent in 2024, still short of the 40 per cent target set for 2025. To close that gap, we must enforce separation at source, support businesses that recover materials, and treat waste as a resource first and fuel last.
Our rubbish is not just a disposal problem. It is a resource we have yet to use properly.
* The author is affiliated with the AGILE Research Group at the Faculty of Business and Communication, Universiti Malaysia Perlis.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

fd86b99ff025c2e8: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s call for Malaysia and Egypt to expand educational cooperation beyond Islamic studies is strategically sound.
Indeed, it should be understood as part of a larger effort to strengthen Malaysia’s geopolitical depth in the Middle East and North Africa.
Egypt is not merely a centre of Islamic civilisation.
It is one of the nine pivotal states whose affairs can affect the whole region — not unlike Algeria, Turkey, Indonesia, Pakistan, India, South Africa, Brazil and Mexico.
It is a massive Arab and African power whose geography, diplomatic influence and control of the Suez Canal make it indispensable to international trade and regional security.
President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi’s state visit to Malaysia on Oct 10, 2026, is more than just another diplomatic exchange.
It offers both countries an opportunity to elevate their longstanding relationship into a comprehensive strategic partnership.

Anwar’s emphasis on engineering, medicine, electrical and electronics, artificial intelligence and digital technology reflects an appreciation that modern diplomacy must combine intellectual cooperation with economic and technological capabilities.
Al-Azhar University will remain central to Malaysia’s religious and educational relationship with Egypt.
Its intellectual tradition of moderation, or “wasatiyyah”, continues to provide an important foundation for Islamic scholarship.
Yet bilateral cooperation cannot remain confined to religious education when the geopolitical environment surrounding both countries has become increasingly complicated.
Malaysia needs strategic depth beyond Southeast Asia.

This means cultivating durable relationships with countries capable of providing diplomatic access, economic opportunities, technological collaboration and strategic understanding across several regions.
Egypt offers precisely such an opportunity.
Situated at the intersection of Africa, especially the Horn of Africa, Mediterranean and the Middle East, Egypt occupies a geographical position that few countries can replicate.
Its control of the Suez Canal gives Cairo enormous strategic relevance.
The canal connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, making it one of the world’s most important maritime passages.
For Malaysia, whose economy depends heavily on international trade, disruptions along this corridor can produce serious consequences.
The Red Sea cannot be understood separately from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects it to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
Persistent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against maritime traffic have demonstrated how non-state actors can threaten international shipping, insurance costs and energy security.
Further east, the Strait of Hormuz remains another critical maritime chokepoint through which substantial quantities of global oil and liquefied natural gas move.

Although Egypt does not control either Bab el-Mandeb or Hormuz, its diplomatic networks and proximity to the Red Sea make it an important partner in understanding these interconnected vulnerabilities.
Malaysia must therefore develop a more sophisticated strategic appreciation of the Middle East and North Africa, the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz.
Such understanding cannot be acquired through occasional diplomatic visits alone.
It requires sustained cooperation among universities, maritime institutions, defence establishments, intelligence analysts and diplomatic academies.
Joint research on maritime security, supply-chain resilience, energy transportation and regional conflict management would provide immediate benefits.
Malaysia and Egypt could establish specialised academic programmes examining how instability in West Asia affects Southeast Asian economies.
Their universities could also cooperate in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, medicine, semiconductor technologies and renewable energy.
These initiatives would help transform educational exchanges into instruments of long-term strategic capacity.
The economic foundations are also already strengthening.
Malaysia could use Egypt as a gateway into African and Mediterranean markets, while Egypt could benefit from Malaysia’s established industrial networks and connections throughout Asean.
Both countries should also deepen defence dialogue, particularly in maritime awareness, military education and professional training.
This need not imply a military alliance. Strategic partnerships can strengthen resilience without creating unnecessary security obligations.
Malaysia’s foreign policy has traditionally emphasised non-alignment, constructive engagement and Asean centrality.
Closer cooperation with Egypt would complement rather than contradict these principles.
Indeed, Asean’s strategic interests increasingly extend beyond its immediate geographical boundaries.
Disruptions in the Red Sea or Hormuz can affect Malaysian manufacturers, exporters, consumers and energy markets.
Geographical distance no longer guarantees economic insulation.
The proposed Malaysia-Egypt strategic partnership should consequently be measured not by ceremonial declarations but by tangible institutional achievements.
Joint research centres, student exchanges, investment projects, maritime dialogues and coordinated diplomatic initiatives would demonstrate genuine progress.
Ultimately, Malaysia and Egypt possess complementary strengths.

Egypt offers geographical centrality, diplomatic experience and access to Africa and the Arab world. Malaysia contributes technological capabilities, industrial experience and connectivity to Southeast Asia.

By moving decisively beyond Islamic studies while preserving their historical educational bonds, both countries can construct a partnership capable of navigating an increasingly uncertain international order.
For Malaysia, strategic depth in the Middle East and North Africa is no longer a diplomatic luxury. It is becoming a geopolitical necessity.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

dfc26074710e0a83: SEOUL, Oct 15 — North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said today.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without “any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries”.
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.

Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing “aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems” and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.

The tests showed the “high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK,” the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country’s official name.

Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water’s surface.
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.

Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea’s arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty. — AFP
4df4feaab2fa6fc4: LONDON: Gold prices were nearly steady on Thursday after touching a one-week low in the previous session as hot inflation data boosted expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike this month.
Spot gold was little changed at US$4,114.57 per ounce, as of 0007 GMT, after hitting its lowest level since Oct 7 on Wednesday. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.7 per cent to US$4,136.10.
US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.

1568dc19c5b55830: OCTOBER 15 — Over the years, I have spent enough money replacing mobile phones that, looking back, I could probably have saved enough for the down payment on a car.
Each new phone came with better technology, more sophisticated features and the brief excitement of owning something new.
Somehow, I hardly use half of these features and probably never will.
Each new phone promises to make my life easier, although I suspect I still use it much as I did 10 years ago.
Manufacturers keep adding features, while my ability to appreciate them remains remarkably unchanged.
Unfortunately, this fascination with new technology appears to have found its way into public policymaking. Announcing something technologically sophisticated certainly sounds impressive.
Whether it actually solves the problem sometimes seems to be a question for another day.
Budget 2027 came with its fair share of welcome announcements. But as with shopping, not everything that looks attractive at first glance necessarily represents good value for money.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that road safety will not improve simply by mandating more sophisticated technology unless authorities first use existing data effectively to identify and correct unsafe driving. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
Some initiatives may eventually become costly distractions, imposing additional obligations on businesses without delivering the improvements that justified them.
The recently announced requirement for commercial vehicles to install telematics systems is one such concern.

The government announced that telematics would be made mandatory to monitor vehicle speed, location and risky driving behaviour, including integration with alcohol detection devices. It sounds impressive and reassuring, particularly when road safety remains a serious public concern.
My concern is particularly with the trucking industry, where operators have been using GPS monitoring systems for years.

Modern systems, especially those equipped with additional sensors and monitoring features, can already capture vehicle speed, location, harsh braking, rapid acceleration and other potentially unsafe driving patterns.
This information provides a valuable foundation for identifying and addressing many driver safety risks. Yet, where is the evidence demonstrating how effectively this information has been utilised?
How many speeding alerts have resulted in corrective action? How many repeat offenders have been identified and dealt with?
More importantly, what improvements in driving behaviour have been achieved?
Advanced telematics certainly offers additional capabilities, particularly in detecting driver fatigue and distraction.
But if we have yet to demonstrate that we can effectively analyse and act upon relatively straightforward GPS data, how prepared are we to manage larger volumes of more sophisticated information?

Some may argue that road safety is too important to question additional government intervention. I would argue that this is precisely why we must ensure that every intervention produces meaningful results.
Before recommending more sophisticated systems, perhaps the Ministry of Transport (MOT) could first show us what has been achieved with the existing ones.
After all, the GPS devices have been doing their job collecting information. Perhaps it is time we demonstrated what we have achieved with that information.

It would come as no surprise to me if, one fine day, after truck operators have invested in sophisticated telematics systems, we are told that even this advanced technology has failed to deliver the expected improvements in road safety.
I consider this a likely outcome if we continue to neglect the need for proactive intervention to correct unsafe driving behaviour.
By then, the equipment will have been installed, the bills paid, and perhaps another technological solution will be waiting to be introduced.
For truck operators already facing rising costs, this is hardly an exciting prospect. The technology keeps advancing, the bills keep arriving, but the problem may remain much the same.
Road safety is not simply about the majority of truck operators and drivers who already comply with safety requirements.

The real challenge is identifying those who fail to comply and ensuring that corrective action is taken. The ministry should first establish whether the required GPS systems are actually installed, functioning and being properly monitored.

If we are still struggling to ensure compliance with these basic requirements, what makes us believe that introducing telematics will be any different? We may simply end up with more sophisticated equipment and the same old enforcement problems.
The priority should be to identify and act against non-compliant operators and unsafe drivers, rather than imposing additional equipment costs on those who are already complying.
After all, installing more gadgets in compliant trucks will not automatically make non-compliant operators any safer.

Once we can demonstrate that existing GPS data is being proactively analysed, unsafe driving behaviour corrected and measurable safety improvements achieved, we will be better positioned to determine what additional technology is necessary.
After all, buying a more sophisticated phone does not automatically make its owner any smarter. The same principle applies to managing road safety.
Our problem is not a shortage of data, but a failure to translate available data into preventive action.
* Chandra Mohan Sinnandavar is a Logistics and Supply Chain professional.

12c8f9b546957daa: JAKARTA, Oct 15 — A female orangutan who was likely starving was evacuated yesterday from an area razed by fire on the Indonesian island of Borneo, officials said, as the country rescues hundreds of animals affected by the blazes.
Indonesia has for weeks struggled to control fires that have razed parts of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua islands, sending choking smog wafting across the border to Malaysia and Singapore.
The orangutan was spotted in a burned forest area in Central Kalimantan province on the Indonesian side of Borneo, local natural resources agency chief Muriansyah told reporters yesterday.
“We strongly suspect that the orangutan was looking for food and then it was seen by residents, who then reported it to officials,” said Muriansyah, who like many Indonesians goes by one name.
The animal, estimated to be around 20 years old, was transferred to an agency facility.
The great ape was anaesthetized so she could be safely captured, with rescuers using a net to collect the sleepy animal from atop a tree, according to an AFP reporter on the scene.

Preliminary examinations showed the female orangutan was not injured and did not appear to be suffering from respiratory problems, said Ichlasul Khaerul, a medical staffer with Orangutan Foundation International (OFI).
However, “seen from her abdominal circumference, probably the orangutan, Ira, was in the state of starvation,” Ichlasul said.
Indonesia has rescued 232 wild animals as of October 8, including 76 proboscis monkeys and 71 orangutans on Borneo, a forestry ministry spokesman said Wednesday.
Orangutans are critically endangered. Around 104,000 remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned fires were burning in habitats containing 52 percent of Borneo’s orangutan population. — AFP

Maghnes Akliouche briefly restored PSG’s three-goal lead in the second half, while Ferran Torres also missed a late penalty for the visitors.
“We try to win every single match. We try to score. We don’t stop if we score one or two goals,” added Luis Enrique.
“It’s very nice to feel that but I have to repeat, today we were lucky because in the second half we could have conceded more goals.”
Enzo Maresca had made a perfect start to the daunting challenge of replacing Pep Guardiola as City manager by winning his first eight games in all competitions.

0efd8fb32ee6ddc6: ROME, Oct 15 — Jose Mourinho hit out at the “shameless” decision by Spanish football authorities to announce that Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior had been slapped with a four-match ban just hours before their Champions League clash with Roma kicked off.
The Brazil international was handed the punishment yesterday after being sent off during Saturday’s 1-0 La Liga win over Villarreal for pulling the hair of an opponent.

It is a costly ban, depriving Mourinho of one of his star attackers for an important run of league games that includes a Clasico clash with rivals Barcelona, who hold a six-point lead over Real at the summit of the table.
Vinicius started as Mourinho’s side pulled off an incredible late comeback to beat Roma 4-3 in the Champions League, having trailed 3-1 with seven minutes remaining.
But the Portuguese made his feelings clear about how the timing of the announcement had disrupted preparations in a post-match press conference.

Mourinho said: “Do you think it’s normal that a player from a Spanish team, who has to play a match that is also important for Spanish football, that two hours before the match a player knows he’s been given a four-match suspension?
“Couldn’t they do it now? Couldn’t they do it tomorrow morning? Do we have to come by bus and almost arrive at the stadium when we find out Vinicius has a four-match suspension?”
Mourinho added: “They do things shamelessly now. The cat is out of the bag now. Two hours before the match, a player must know he has a four-match suspension.

“A Spanish team that has earned three points for Spanish football, for the rankings, for the prestige of Spanish football. You want to kill a player two hours before the match; it doesn’t seem normal to me.”
Scheduling complaints
Mourinho also highlighted his unhappiness with scheduling, with his side set to face AEK Athens in the Greek capital on 4 November, before travelling to Valencia in La Liga on 7 November.
Asked what the Vinicius ban announcement says, Mourinho replied: “At the very least, a lack of respect.
“Playing in Athens last night, arriving in Madrid probably at 5am, something like that, and then playing Saturday in Valencia, on a weekend that precedes a week of national team matches.
“It makes absolutely no sense, they make you play on Saturday in Valencia, which is an extremely difficult match, it doesn’t seem innocent to me.

“The usual excuses, I don’t buy them, because this wasn’t 25 years ago. The excuses from TV, that it was TV that decided, that it was TV that chose the match for Saturday, I don’t buy this anymore. I’m too old to swallow this.

“And this Vinicius story, two hours before a match, knowing that he has a four-match suspension, doesn’t deserve comment. Real Madrid fans aren’t stupid and I will do everything possible to open people’s eyes.”
It was a good night for Mourinho on the pitch, as his substitutions turned the game in Real’s favour after they were outplayed for much of the game until the closing stages.

Donyell Malen’s double had given Roma a 3-1 lead early in the second half, but two of Mourinho’s substitutes scored, Endrick and Carlos Espi, and another, Arda Guler, provided two assists in the late rally.
“I’m not going to be a genius and say I had prepared everything for a 3-1 to 4-3 victory, it’s not true,” Mourinho said.
“But I genuinely thought that in the last 20 minutes I had substitutions I could make, and I had substitutions that could change things.” — AFP
524b8c66c63269a5: SAN ISIDRO, Oct 15 — Diego Maradona’s family yesterday called for his medical team to be given stiff prison terms over what two of his daughters called his “murder.”

dbdeeb455657e880: OCTOBER 15 — On September 10, 1963, six days before the Federation of Malaya would be abolished and a new Federation of Malaysia established, the Government of the State of Kelantan commenced proceedings in the High Court for declarations that the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) and the Malaysia Act 1963 (Act 1963) were null and void or alternatively were not binding on the State of Kelantan.

The State of Kelantan contended that (a) Act 1963, which received the Royal Assent on August 26, 1963, violated the Federation of Malaya Agreement 1957 (Malayan Agreement); (b) the proposed changes needed the consent of each of the constituent States, including Kelantan, and this had not been obtained; (c) the Ruler of Kelantan should have been a party to MA63; (d) constitutional convention called for consultation with Rulers of individual States as to substantial changes to be made to the Federation of Malaya Constitution 1957 (Merdeka Constitution); and (e) the Federal Parliament had no power to legislate for Kelantan in respect of any matter regarding which that State had its own legislature.
In the course of his judgment, the first Chief Justice of Malaya James Beveridge Thomson (later Lord President of the Federal Court) said as follows:
“[T]he two things which are attacked in the present proceedings are the action of Parliament in enacting [Act 1963] Act and the action of the Government in concluding MA63.

“In each case the [challenge] lies [against] the admission of the three new States and the change of name without the [Government of the State of Kelantan] having been consulted. It is conceded that it has not in fact been consulted although it clearly had prior knowledge (as distinct from notice in the technical sense) of what was proposed.

“These things, it is said, will in effect transmogrify the present Federation of Malaya into an entirely new and different Federation known as Malaysia. This may or may not be true. In my view, however, it is beside the point and is nothing but a playing with words.

“The real question is not whether any such radical change will in fact result from what has been done by Parliament and the Executive Government but whether Parliament or the Executive Government has trespassed in any way the limits placed on their powers by the [Merdeka] Constitution.

“These powers were given by the signatories to the [Malayan Agreement]and they have not been taken away. If the steps that have been taken are in all respects lawful the nature of the results they have produced cannot of itself make them unlawful. Fiat justitia, ruat coelum! [Let justice be done, though the heavens fall]
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The author argues that constitutional provisions and contractual clauses must be interpreted in their full legal context, rather than read selectively or in isolation. — Pexels pic
The Chief Justice then continued:
“Let us examine the relevant powers of Parliament and of the Executive as they are set out in the [Merdeka] Constitution.

“By Article 2 Parliament may by law ‘admit other States to the Federation’. Then by Article 74, as read with the Ninth Schedule, Parliament may, without prejudice to any power to make laws conferred on it by any other Article, make laws relating to a large number of subjects.

“Among these are external affairs (including the making of treaties, agreements and conventions) defence, internal security and the machinery of Government. If any State law is inconsistent with any law made by Parliament then, by reason of Article 75, the law made by Parliament is to prevail and the State law is pro tanto void, and by Article 76 Parliament may make laws on subjects which would otherwise be out with its competence if they are made for the purpose of implementing any treaty or agreement between the Federation and any other country.

“By Article 160 the [Merdeka] Constitution itself is a written law and by Article 159 Parliament may make laws amending its provisions. This power is subject only to the restriction that a Bill to amend the [Merdeka] Constitution requires to be passed by a majority of each House of Parliament consisting of two-thirds of the total number of members and by reason of Article 159(5) a law amending Articles 38, 70 or 71(1), which deal with the position of Their Highnesses the Rulers, or amending Article 153, which relates to the special position of the Malays, shall not be enacted without the consent of the Conference of Rulers.

“It is, however, to be noted that by reason of Article 159 the requirement of a two-thirds majority does not apply to any amendment of the [Merdeka] Constitution made for or in connection with the admission of any State.
“It has not even been suggested that [Act 1963] was not passed strictly in accordance with the provisions of the [Merdeka] Constitution relating to Acts amending the Constitution.

“It amended Article 1(1) which provides that ‘the Federation shall be known by the name of Persekutuan Tanah Melayu (in English the Federation of Malaya)’ by providing [in Section 4(1)] that ‘the Federation shall be known, in Malay and in English, by the name Malaysia’.
“It amended Article 1(2) by adding [in Section 4(2)] the States of Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to the States originally enumerated in Article 1(2).

“In doing these things I cannot see that Parliament went in any way beyond its powers or that it did anything so fundamentally revolutionary as to require fulfilment of a condition which the [Merdeka] Constitution itself does not prescribe — that is to say a condition to the effect that the State of Kelantan or any other State should be consulted.

“It is true in a sense that the new Federation is something different from the old one. It will contain more States. It will have a different name. But if that state of affairs be brought about by means contained in the [Merdeka] Constitution itself and which were contained in it at the time of the [Malayan Agreement], of which it is an integral part, I cannot see how it can possibly be made out that there has been any breach of any foundation pact among the original parties.
“In bringing about these changes Parliament has done no more than exercise the powers which were given to it in [Malayan Agreement] by the constituent States including the State of Kelantan.”
Two more provisions of the Merdeka Constitution were referred to by the Chief Justice in the following paragraphs:

“[B]y Article 39 the executive authority of the Federation is vested in the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and is exercisable, subject to the provisions of any federal law and with certain exceptions, by him or by the Cabinet or any Minister authorised by the Cabinet.

“By Article 80(1) the executive authority of the Federation extends to all matters with respect to which Parliament may make laws which, as has been seen, includes external affairs including treaties and agreements.

“[MA63] is signed ‘for the Federation of Malaya’ by the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister and four other members of the Cabinet. There is nothing whatsoever in the [Merdeka] Constitution requiring consultation with any State Government or the Ruler of any State.
“[Accordingly], a power has been lawfully exercised by the body to which that power was given by the States in 1957.”

In the circumstances, the Chief Justice refused the declarations that the State of Kelantan sought – that is, that MA63 and Act 1963 were null and void or alternatively were not binding on the State of Kelantan.

The decision was delivered on September 14 — two days before Malaysia Day. (See the case of The Government of the State of Kelantan v Government of the Federation of Malaya and Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj [1963])
What needs to be highlighted from the judgement as set out in extensio above is this: no provision of a written law or a clause in an agreement can be read in isolation.
When the Chief Justice said “Let us examine” it means examining the relevant provisions as they are set out in the written law — that is, the Constitution, Act, Ordinance and Enactment.
Thus, Article 1(1) (on the name of the Federation) and Article 1(2) (on the States of the Federation) must be read together with Article 159 (on amendment of the Constitution).

In the case Re Datuk James Wong Kim, Minister of Home Affairs, Malaysia & Ors v Datuk James Wong Kim Min, it was a pre-Malaysia state Ordinance that must not be read in isolation but read together with Article 159A of the Constitution (on operation of transitional provisions of the Malaysia Act 1963).
In the case of Reddy v Employees Provident Fund Board [1967], it was a pre-Merdeka state Ordinance that must not be read in isolation but together with Article 160 (on interpretation of words).
The same goes for agreement: read an agreement wholly — that is, to the full or entire extent. Don’t read its clauses in isolation.
No provision of a written law and no clause in an agreement can be read in isolation.
