b88b21b5c829ef7a: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.

The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones, robotic landers, communication satellites, and a nuclear power plant; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.

Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”

The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?

But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.
SELMAN DESIGN

But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?

The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.

Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”

Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.
The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe.
Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.

The first is galactic cosmic rays, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.

Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.

The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.

As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.

Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.

Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover.

How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says Nicholas Schmerr, a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes.

Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer.

That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by ramming into the rock with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-­edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or entirely vaporize errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to spy killers—such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years.

All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what?

It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.”
Having your base destroyed by an asteroid would be awful. But a moon base is far more likely to be imperiled by dust—which, unlike asteroids, is everywhere, all the time.

Volcanic lunar rocks, when broken down, turn into sharp, electrostatically charged, adhesive, acrid, abrasive particles. While on the moon, Apollo astronauts who inhaled some of this dust occasionally suffered from a strange “lunar hay fever,” which irritated their eyes and agitated their lungs. That same dust ate through all kinds of gear with disturbing ease. “It rips up seals, gears, motors, spacesuits, habitats—everything else it comes into contact with,” says Justin Cyrus, the CEO of Lunar Outpost, a spaceflight technology company that is providing NASA with one of the Artemis program’s moon rovers.

NASA has already developed a defense against these dark shards: the electrodynamic dust shield, or EDS. The lightweight electrodes that make up this shield—which can be layered on machinery, walls, and perhaps even spacesuits—use opposing currents to blast away the electrically charged dust. The EDS worked wonders when tested in labs on Earth, and it also demonstrated its anti-dust magic when sent to the lunar surface in 2025 as part of a NASA-sponsored robotic mission.

Amy Fritz, a dust-mitigation researcher at Johnson Space Center, says that the EDS will likely be widely featured all over a lunar habitat. But other dust-fighting instruments are being developed too—including a lint-roller-type object inspired by gecko skin and a sci-fi-esque blaster that uses ionized nitrogen gas. Its first spray will neutralize the charge of the dust to remove its stickiness; then a second burst will clear it off the surface.

Irritatingly, the busier a base gets, the dustier things will become. As it expands to the size of a small city, rocket ships will need to deliver cargo and crew to the lunar surface on a frequent cadence. Each takeoff and landing will launch a salvo of dust in every direction, inundating the base’s infrastructure. “You have to worry about essentially being sandblasted every time,” says Fritz.

Metzger calculates that even with landing pads more than 3,000 feet away from a base, just 10 to 20 liftoffs or landings would be sufficient to severely damage things like protective coatings on exterior walls and communications equipment. After a while, he says, “everything breaks.”

Even if the moon base of the future is buried partly below ground, barricaded against micrometeorites and space radiation, and well equipped with dust-repelling technologies, it’s still a risky gig for any astronaut. Skipping around in a preternaturally agile way at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity will be entertaining. But “microgravity is not good for the human body,” says Dreyer. Muscle wastage, cardiovascular troubles, respiratory problems, and immune deficiencies can arise.

Radiation, too, may always afflict lunar residents. And there’s also evidence that disease-causing microbes could stealthily sneak aboard spacecraft, even after stringent sterilization procedures. Those microbes may behave differently than they do on Earth; microgravity experiments (both real and simulated) have suggested that some become more aggressive and more likely to cause disease. “We call them the invisible crew,” says Lisa Carnell, the director of NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division.
NASA/GSFC/MIT

Hoping to find a better way to protect astronauts, Carnell spearheaded an experiment called AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response), which launched aboard the Artemis II mission. It used thumb-drive-size chips, containing cells taken from the heart, lungs, or other parts of the body, that could be switched on to act like miniature organs. Scientists have previously used this organ-on-a-chip technology for purposes like testing out new pharmaceuticals in a highly controlled setting. For Artemis II, Carnell’s crew sent up chips containing bone marrow samples taken from the mission’s four astronauts. Bone marrow makes red and white blood cells, as well as platelets—the sort of stuff that affects almost the entire human body. So seeing how space radiation and microgravity affect it would give Carnell and her team vital insight into how astronauts’ biology might change on the moon.

The advantage of organ chips is that you can make them for any astronaut and then send them into space ahead of time to see how that person’s organs will react to spaceflight. Researchers envision that data from such chips will be able to clue medics in to the specific preventive treatments or pharmaceuticals that will help moonbound astronauts on their journey.

What is NASA likely to send up sooner rather than later? “Brain organoids,” says Carnell. Yes, she adds—that sounds super weird. But it would be good to know how a real brain might respond to being on the moon for several months before people start living there.

Okay. Your vast moon base and its inhabitants are protected—as much as is possible—from the treacherous lunar environment. But astronauts’ time is extremely valuable, and humans are fragile creatures. You can’t make them do all the heavy lifting, which means that whether you’re trying to make a tiny lunar outpost or a small city, you’re going to need a lot of robots. “The buildup of the moon base, in the first years, will pretty much 99% be robotic,” says NASA’s García-Galán.

Autonomy will be there right from the start. NASA’s new version of the moon buggy, its Lunar Terrain Vehicle, can be driven by the astronauts riding in it but can also be piloted remotely from Earth (or from elsewhere on the moon). There are visions, too, of adding modular robotic arms, towing vehicles, and cargo movers—all still in the preliminary stages of planning.

Over the next few decades, though, we’ll likely want an army of robots to do our bidding: excavators to dig up lunar rocks that could be turned into concrete and bricks, plus other robots to flatten surfaces, dig trenches, create building foundations, pave landing pads, and build up dust-deflecting berms to keep the base from being sandblasted by launches and landings. Even solar panels and wiring can potentially be made from moon rocks—something that the spaceflight company Blue Origin demonstrated in labs on Earth in 2023 using a geologic simulant designed to match the composition of lunar regolith.

Powering this robot army will require considerable energy. Two-week-long nights make solar power an impractical solution. Aside from a cornucopia of high-­capacity, extreme-temperature-resistant batteries, nuclear power is probably the only viable option. A small, car-size nuclear reactor, filled with an almost literal handful of uranium, could power a small village for a decade without needing to be refueled. And although nobody’s yet tested a nuclear reactor on the moon, few doubt that NASA and the US Department of Energy can conjure up a working design—one that perhaps wouldn’t be too different from those aboard nuclear submarines. A moon base in 2100 would probably feature multiple small, autonomously or remotely operated nuclear reactors, which—conveniently—the base-expanding robots could simply plug themselves into to recharge.

But the biggest lunar question mark might be water, which planners want to support the astronauts—and to make fuel to launch things from the lunar surface. A process known as electrolysis, which uses electricity to snap apart molecular bonds, can be used to split water into oxygen and hydrogen, both of which could be used to make rocket fuel. Getting them this way could be far less expensive than sending either all the way from Earth. And as an added bonus, it would provide a source of breathable oxygen.

Orbital data has revealed that there is some amount of water preserved in patches on the lunar south pole, but little is known about how much there actually is, what form it takes, or how easy it will be to extract. Will there be solid sheets of ice here and there, ready for us to excavate? Or will there be scattered ice crystals intermingled among the rocky grains, requiring some more inventive form of extraction?
dabcea560a219927: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.

Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.

Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.

That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba, hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.

The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.
Filling in the gaps

Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees, after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way?

While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs, Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land.

Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow.

In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.

The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.

For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia-dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.
To plant or not to plant

Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun.

Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest.

“Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.”

In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded.
Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness.

The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting.

Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal.

There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape.

The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.”
Matthew Ponsford is a freelance reporter based in London.
7af8688e509420ee: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah

Last week, I attended a screening of Man Who Walked the Talk: The Tun Razak Story. As I watched his life unfold, something dawned on me. My thoughts returned to the Hukum Kanun Pahang, the manuscript I had spent so much time studying, and to the responsibilities of the Shahbandar within its account of government.
I began to see Tun Razak’s life through another lens: the tradition of service from which he came.
In an interview after the screening, I said, “It is in their blood, from one generation to another.”

I meant the understanding of responsibility that can grow within a family over generations. A child observes how his father serves, listens to the matters discussed around him and gradually learns what public office demands.

We understand this in a royal household. A prince learns something of the art of kingship by observing his father long before he is called upon to exercise it. Watching the documentary, I realised that a similar education took place in the household of a Shahbandar.
Tun Abdul Razak was himself the tenth Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar.
The Shahbandar had become Prime Minister.
There was something deeply moving in that thought. A son of Pahang had carried his upbringing, experience and understanding of duty into the service of an entire nation.

In Pahang, the Orang Besar Berempat comprises the Orang Kaya Indera Perba Jelai, Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar, Orang Kaya Indera Pahlawan and Orang Kaya Indera Segara. Each held responsibilities within the administration of the state, with a particular territory under his authority.

They supported the ruler in governing: offering counsel, administering affairs and exercising the authority entrusted to them. In modern terms, aspects of their work might be compared to the responsibilities of ministers. Their offices belonged, however, to a different political order, and were distinct from succession to the throne.
Of these four titles familiar to us in Pahang today, it was the Shahbandar that I encountered in my study of the Hukum Kanun Melaka and the Hukum Kanun Pahang.

That recognition returned to me during the screening. The Shahbandar was already an important officer in the world described by those legal texts. Centuries later, a man bearing that title would lead Malaysia.

The earlier office and the later hereditary Pahang title must be understood in their respective historical settings. Yet the connection invites us to look more closely at the traditions of government from which Tun Razak emerged.

There is an important distinction to make. The Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar holds office by royal appointment of the Sultan of Pahang. Although the title has remained within the same family across generations, it does not pass automatically from father to son.
Generations of Shahbandars have served Pahang’s rulers, offering counsel and assisting in the affairs of government according to the responsibilities of their time.
Across generations, this relationship has carried a continuing responsibility: to support the ruler in serving Pahang and its people.
Tun Razak was the tenth holder. His son, Najib, became the eleventh, and his grandson, Nizar, the twelfth.
The Sultan appoints the officeholder. The family can help prepare him to fulfil its responsibilities.
That preparation is what interests me.

A son growing up in such a household could observe how his father advised the ruler, received those seeking assistance and dealt with the affairs of the state. He could learn how to listen, how to weigh competing concerns and how to carry the expectations attached to the family’s position.
Just as a prince could learn the art of kingship from his father, a future Shahbandar could learn the responsibilities of government and service from him.

This is an inheritance that does not appear neatly in a family tree. Genealogy records names, relationships and the succession of titles. The knowledge passed through daily example is harder to trace, but deserves our attention.

The family’s history in Pahang reaches back to 1722 and to forebears who came from Sulawesi. That migration also carried knowledge and craftsmanship, including the weaving tradition associated with Tenun Pahang. The similarities between the textiles of Pahang and Sulawesi bear witness to a shared cultural history.

For me, this connection has particular meaning. My work with Tenun Pahang has taught me how knowledge survives through people: through hands that demonstrate, eyes that observe and younger generations willing to learn.
My study of the Hukum Kanun Pahang has brought me to another form of knowledge, the understanding of authority, duty and the ordering of a state.

At the screening, those two strands of my own work came together in an unexpected way. I found myself thinking about what families carry across generations, whether in craftsmanship or public service, and how that inheritance can find new expression.

Tun Razak succeeded his father as Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar in 1950. He became Pahang State Secretary in 1952 and Menteri Besar in 1955. His subsequent career took him to the offices of Deputy Prime Minister and Prime Minister of Malaysia.
His field of responsibility grew, from the affairs of Pahang to the affairs of a nation.

When I say that he carried Pahang to Malaysia, I mean that he brought something of his formation in Pahang into national service. His roots remained part of him as he undertook responsibilities far beyond the state from which he came.
Every appointment nevertheless demanded his own ability, judgment and commitment. An upbringing could prepare him; the work remained his to do.
That is why the documentary’s title is so fitting. Man Who Walked the Talk directs us to the actions through which he fulfilled his responsibilities.

Watching it, I saw both the man’s achievements and a question about his formation. What had he learned from the generations before him? What understanding of service had he absorbed in the household where he grew up? How might that experience have shaped the way he approached government?
These are questions worth exploring alongside the familiar record of his education and political career.

For me, the Hukum Kanun Pahang has made the offices of our earlier government more visible. Behind each title stood a person entrusted with responsibilities. Behind that person might stand generations of experience, remembered and taught within a family.
I had gone to watch a documentary about Tun Razak. I came away reflecting on the inheritance of an art: the art of governing, learned through example and proved through service.
The Shahbandar had become Prime Minister.
And a tradition of responsibility rooted in Pahang had found a larger field of service in Malaysia.
May Allah grant Tun Abdul Razak His mercy and reward him for the good he brought to the people.
Al-Fatihah.

Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia, and is currently a PhD candidate at ISTAC-IIUM.
19640f019f148359: Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington in September produced no major new agreement. But it did result in an extension of the trade truce that Xi and US president Donald Trump struck in Busan, South Korea, last October.
Instead of expiring on Nov 10, the truce will expire on Jan 10, 2027. Though modest, this achievement has given an unstable world economy a reprieve.

The core agreement is simple enough: China will refrain from enforcing the export controls on rare earths and related materials that it unveiled last October, and the US will refrain from raising tariffs further, holding the overall duty on Chinese goods near the 47% level reached in Busan (down from 57% beforehand).
Both sides have grumbled about compliance, but neither wants the truce to lapse before the presidents meet again, first in Shenzhen in November, then the following month in Miami.

China clearly has a great deal of leverage in dealing with Trump. It accounts for roughly 60–70% of global rare-earth mining and 85–90% of rare-earth processing (the step that turns mixed ores into the oxides used in many critical technologies).

And when it comes to the heavy rare-earth elements, China’s grip is even tighter. Processing of dysprosium and terbium, essential ingredients in electric-vehicle magnets, wind turbines, and missile-guidance systems, is carried out almost exclusively in China.

On a detailed element-by-element accounting, the US and its allies have meaningful non-Chinese extraction capacity for only seven or eight of the 17 rare earths, but essentially no processing capacity. That could change in the next two years, with the processing figure growing to five elements.

The Australian miner Lynas and the US-based MP Materials already ship commercial volumes of lighter elements like neodymium and praseodymium, and within ten years, non-Chinese extraction could cover nearly all light elements and most heavy ones.

But even then, the processing figure may reach only nine elements, with dysprosium and terbium remaining overwhelmingly under Chinese control. While future innovations in processing, or in designing rare earths out of manufactured goods altogether, could alter the picture, such scenarios are harder to predict.
It is also useful to question the belief that “de-risking” from China would leave the US and Europe unambiguously better off. Recent geopolitical developments suggest otherwise.
Now that the US no longer wants to be bound by international rules that it considers inconvenient, rare-earth leverage is one of the few remaining restraints on US protectionism and economic warfare.

Since the Trump administration seems oblivious to the cost of tariffs on US households, there is no guarantee that the next round of tariffs would stop at a level Americans can comfortably bear. In fact, by threatening to reduce, but not eliminate, the rare-earth supply, China may be saving Trump from himself, at least in the short term.
The European Union (EU) faces a similar situation. It has been more cautious than the US about raising tariffs on Chinese goods, partly because European industry is heavily reliant on Chinese inputs.
Although the EU’s own Critical Raw Materials Act targets 40% domestic processing by 2030, its auditors reported in February that actual capacity remains near 25%.

Tellingly, although Japan has spent over a decade and roughly US$1.2 billion diversifying away from China since a 2010 rare-earths dispute, its heavy rare-earth imports collapsed by 70–80% in early 2026.

Export controls were not invented by the Chinese. The US commerce department’s entity list has grown roughly ninefold over the past decade, to nearly 1,200 entries, while China’s own retaliatory lists have grown only through the occasional addition of a few dozen entities at a time. On this measure, the US and the EU currently maintain considerably longer control lists than China does.

Although export controls are nominally aimed at military applications, the national-security rationale is not always as clean as advertised, and the civilian collateral damage often rivals the intended effect.

In the case of the US and Chinese export controls, one unintended consequence has been a reduction in US exports and Chinese imports. This is probably because export controls cut off Chinese customers from US suppliers, who mostly failed to find replacement buyers and instead suffered a loss of revenue, profitability, and employment.

Whereas Oxford Economics estimates that export controls cost China a cumulative 0.8% of GDP in 2024–26, a 2023 input-output study concludes that the US has, in relative terms, lost more, with Japanese, South Korean, and European firms capturing the resulting market share.

In a world where the rules-based trading system is not functioning, a fragile status quo stabilised by mutual leverage is probably better than unilateral acts of dominance or chaos. If the zero-sum wrangling ultimately inspires a return to multilateral negotiation, so much the better.

Shang-Jin Wei, a former chief economist at the Asian Development Bank, is professor of finance and economics at Columbia Business School and Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.

f23750c0294ac548: In my previous column, I wrote about LIDAC26, the Luno Institutional Digital Asset Conference hosted by cryptocurrency exchange Luno in Kuala Lumpur on Sept 24, and confessed that my favourite session had nothing to do with regulators or stablecoins.
It was a breakout on Malaysian builders shaping the global digital asset landscape, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since.

Here's why. Talking to participants and reading reports, I found that if you have ever checked the price of a coin, traced a transaction on Ethereum or swapped one token for another on Solana (two of the world's busiest blockchains), there is a decent chance you used something that started in Malaysia, whether you knew it or not.

That's not just national pride talking: Tiger Research, a crypto research firm, said as much in its 2025 report on our market: "Etherscan, Jupiter, Virtuals Protocol, and CoinGecko all started in Malaysia and now have global reach."
The crypto world's price list

Start with CoinGecko, which Bobby Ong, an economics graduate of University College London, and TM Lee, who studied computer science at Purdue University, founded in Kuala Lumpur in April 2014. It began by tracking a mere 20 coins and now covers more than 21,000 crypto assets across over 1,000 exchanges, drawing what it says are more than 10 million users a month.
What I find most remarkable is how they got there, with no venture capital and no first hire until January 2018.

"Choosing not raising venture capital allowed us the opportunity to not need to relocate to Silicon Valley, one of the most expensive locations to live in," Ong told CryptoSlate in 2021, while Lee put it even more bluntly to The Edge: "There were no parents to bankroll us. We kept it low-cost and kept reinvesting; this helped us stay in the game."

In January, CoinDesk reported that CoinGecko was weighing a sale at a valuation of around RM2 billion. Not bad for a startup whose founders, The Edge reported in 2021, worked remotely before renting their first office in Taman Tun Dr Ismail.
The window into Ethereum
Then there is Etherscan, launched in 2015 by Matthew Tan. Think of it as a search engine for the Ethereum blockchain: punch in a wallet or transaction and it shows you exactly where the money went.

Back in 2019, The Edge reported that Tan was running the business out of Shah Alam with a team of just 15, and that it was already profitable. Since then, Etherscan says it has ranked among the world's top 1,000 websites by traffic, and in 2024 it bought Solscan, a popular explorer for the rival Solana blockchain.

Today, a team of more than 70 runs over 60 explorers, and developers can pull data from more than 50 blockchains with a single Etherscan key. That's right, the explorer Tan built and launched back in 2015 now reaches across much of the crypto world.
Solana's best-price finder

Next up is Jupiter, co-founded by Siong Ong, who sat on that LIDAC panel. Jupiter is an aggregator, which means it scans Solana's many trading venues for the best price and then makes the swap for you, even splitting your order across several venues if that gets you a better deal.

The numbers are staggering: according to data tracker DefiLlama, Jupiter has routed more than RM5 trillion in trades to date, and handled almost RM60 billion in the past 30 days alone, about half of all aggregator volume on Solana.
When Jupiter launched its JUP token in January 2024, it handed out a billion tokens to more than a million wallets, and it has since grown into perpetual futures, lending and a mobile wallet.
And the bench runs deep

Virtuals Protocol, co-founded by Jansen Teng, lets anyone launch and co-own artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Its token briefly topped a market value of RM20 billion in January 2025, and in February this year it launched Eastworld Labs to put humanoid robots to work, because, in Teng's words, they "are currently hamstrung by two fundamental bottlenecks: lack of data and capital".

Virtuals said more than 18,000 AI agents had already been deployed on its platform, alongside a fleet of more than 30 full-sized humanoid robots. Being in the robotics industry myself, I can tell you that is no small feat.

Then there is Pendle, a marketplace that lets investors trade the future yield on their crypto, a little like stripping a bond's coupons from its principal and selling them separately. Binance Labs, then the venture arm of the world's largest crypto exchange, backed it in 2023, and at its peak in September 2025 it held more than RM54 billion in deposits.
Tiger Research counts Pendle among the global projects in which "Malaysian talents also play key roles".

Sure, crypto is volatile, and several of these figures sit well below their peaks today. But the point is not the price of any single token; it is that a country of our size keeps producing the people who build tools much of the industry relies on.

Sitting in that breakout room two weeks ago, it struck me that the three founders on stage had, between them, built the price list, the search engine and the best-price finder that millions of crypto users lean on every day, and that all three companies started right here in Malaysia.
It's about time we celebrated them like the world-class builders they are.

86c42fc21c2ad724: From Khairul Hafezad Abdullah
When a heavy-rain warning appears on our phones, most of us understand what it means. We know which roads usually flood, which rivers may rise, and which neighbourhoods have been affected before.
Yet knowing that a risk exists is not the same as being prepared for it.

After a major flood, we often hear people say: “We never thought it would get this bad.” Often the problem is not always that we failed to see the danger. We saw it, understood it - and carried on as usual.

This is a familiar challenge in safety management. When people are repeatedly exposed to a hazard without serious consequences, their perception of risk can change. What once caused concern begins to feel normal.

Consider a family in a flood-prone area. The water may have reached the front gate several times but never entered the house. This past experience becomes reassurance: “It happens every year. The water will subside."
But the next flood does not have to behave like the last one. A hazard does not become less dangerous simply because we are accustomed to it.

Malaysia today has far better access to information than it did decades ago. Weather warnings reach our phones quickly, while river levels, road closures and evacuation centres can be monitored almost in real time.

The real question is what we do with that information. Do we move vehicles to higher ground, secure important documents and medicines, check on vulnerable family members or neighbours, and know where to go if evacuation becomes necessary? Or do we read the warning, glance outside, and continue as usual?

According to the statistics department, floods caused an estimated RM636.9 million in losses nationwide in 2025. Public assets and infrastructure accounted for RM380.2 million, while damage to living quarters amounted to RM183.8 million.
But preparedness should begin before we start counting losses.
Imagine being told you have 10 minutes to leave your house. What would you take? Who would need assistance? Where would you go? Would everyone know what to do?
For households with elderly people, young children, persons with disabilities or family members requiring regular medication, these questions matter even more.
Communities matter, too. In the first moments of an emergency, rescue personnel cannot be at every doorstep. Sometimes, the first person able to help is a neighbour.
A prepared community knows which households may need assistance, which roads become inaccessible first, and how reliable information can be shared quickly.

From an occupational safety viewpoint, good safety management does not wait for someone to be injured before action is taken. Hazards are identified, risks assessed and reasonable controls are introduced beforehand.
Why should disaster preparedness be any different?

Preparedness does not mean living in constant fear, nor does every warning require panic. It means accepting risk and uncertainty as part of the package, and taking reasonable action before circumstances become critical.
So when the next warning appears on our phones, perhaps the question should not be: “Will it really get that bad?” It should be: “If it does, are we ready to act?”
Khairul Hafezad Abdullah is a senior lecturer in occupational safety and health management, and a reader of FMT.

8d0d8c2963978094: The political backdrop was impossible to ignore as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim presented the 2027 budget.

With the next general elections (GE16) looming in a matter of months, most observers expected a flashier, election-winning plan aimed squarely at capturing votes highlighting the gains of Ekonomi Madani.
Instead, the 2027 budget arrived as a steady, work-a-day, “civil service” budget lacking a dramatic “wow factor”.

Choosing fiscal stability over electoral fireworks is a missed opportunity for a government seeking a renewed mandate but the reality is more nuanced. The complex political landscape of the unity government means a pragmatic, steady-as-she-goes approach was likely the only option Anwar had available.

On paper, the economic fundamentals driving the budget appear robust. Driven by strong macroeconomic growth of 5.7% in the first half of the year, record trade performance and rising investments including RM132 billion in the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, Anwar had room to manoeuvre.
Instead, the budget attempts to continue the dual ambition of “raising the ceiling” and “lifting the floor”.
The minimum wage rises to RM2,000, but only in eight months’ time. The higher RM2,500 benchmark for entry-level graduate positions will benefit a few but not many.

Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) was raised a little for its nine million core recipients and SARA-untuk-Semua was institutionalised with a tiny RM100 twice-yearly credit to the M40.

Meanwhile, civil servants on whom Anwar relies for what remains of his current term of office were given their share as usual. The general public on whom he relies for his next term of office were left wanting.
Higher personal income tax reliefs were finally announced but primarily benefit middle-to-higher income earners rather than lower-income households.
Notably absent was any reinstatement of the goods and services tax (GST), despite calls from business for structural tax reforms like indexed reliefs or alternative electronic payment taxes (EPTs).

Administrative fixes including resolving longstanding contract doctor issues with permanent appointments, launching the MediAsas coverage initiative help in the healthcare sector but there were no big reforms on elderly care.
Directing domestic investment through GLICs into sectors like semiconductors and AI infrastructure is a continuation of existing policies and not a new departure.

For everyday voters looking for immediate relief, the budget may feel underwhelming. The minimum wage increase, while positive, includes exemptions for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and the delayed implementation timeline leaves many low-wage workers feeling overlooked.
Meanwhile, fiscal consolidation metrics such as improved debt and deficit ratios are largely driven by higher GDP growth rather than structural spending cuts in borrowing.

In comparison to bolder shadow budgets and economic reform agendas which advocate for broad universal basic pensions, or expanded progressive wage schemes, this budget takes a conservative path. It held back from sweeping structural overhauls or aggressive handouts.
So, a big question is why did Anwar choose prudence over populism on the eve of an election? The answer lies in coalitional arithmetic.
Anwar leads a multi-coalition government where key partners hold significant leverage.

In the run-up to GE16, coalition allies are cautious about allowing the prime minister to deploy massive, popular pre-election handouts that could boost his popularity at their collective expense in contested seats.
Barisan Nasional does not want Anwar taking credit ahead of the election.
Consequently, the budget is a compromise. An administrative, predictable roadmap managed by fiscal conservatism.
It reassures markets and international investors while keeping the coalition intact.
It may not guarantee an electoral landslide but in the volatile arena of Malaysian politics, a steady hand on the wheel may well be the most realistic strategy Anwar could deploy.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d7c7b91ebc036608: Orang Melayu ada pepatah, sudah terhantuk baru tengadah. Maknanya, apabila sesuatu yang buruk berlaku, barulah kita sedar untuk berbuat sesuatu. Sesuatu yang dibuat itu sudah tentulah perubahan yang agak drastik supaya tidak terhantuk lagi. Namun demikian, dalam kes buli yang mengakibatkan kematian, kecederaan dan trauma, orang Melayu seperti ‘sudah terhantuk terus lali dan tidur’. Sebabnya, banyak insiden yang terpaksa kita tanggung sebagai rakyat dan orang Melayu, tetapi ia tetap berlaku. Selang beberapa hari di Negeri Sembilan yang kini tersohor dengan kemelut pemerintahan tidak berkesudahan, kita dengar kes buli di sekolah berasrama. Ada juga kes buli yang mengakibatkan kematian di sekolah awam, tetapi perkara itu, bagi saya lebih mudah diselesaikan. Saya hendak cuba selesaikan masalah buli di sekolah berasrama dulu sebab ia paling teruk dan memalukan orang Melayu. Sebabnya kita tak pernah dengar kes buli yang mencederakan mangsa, mati atau trauma dari sekolah vernakular Cina atau India. Mungkin sebab sekolah vernakular tidak ada asrama penuh seperti orang Melayu.

Saya mendesak semua sekolah berasrama ditutup, paling kurang enam bulan atau setahun. Sudah tentu akan ada backlash besar daripada ibu bapa yang lebih mementingkan pelajaran. Cadangan saya adalah semua pelajar sekolah berasrama ditempatkan sementara di sekolah awam berdekatan sehingga segala peralatan keselamatan, SOP pentadbiran dan latihan mengenal pasti buli yang disertai semua guru sekolah agama dilaksanakan.

Pertamanya, Kementerian Pendidikan dan Majlis Amanah Rakyat (Mara) perlu membiayai audit di semua sekolah berasrama yang akan dijalankan sebuah firma audit keselamatan paling profesional. Mungkin firma ini mempunyai kriteria audit sendiri, tetapi saya ingin mengemukakan beberapa pemerhatian saya untuk diambil kira.

Pertama, audit perlu dijalankan terhadap keberkesanan penempatan CCTV di tempat strategik, bukan ikut suka pentadbir sekolah. Jumlah dan visual coverage CCTV perlu ditentukan secara khusus dan mengikut kajian mendalam, selain mewujudkan bilik kawalan CCTV oleh pengawal terlatih.

Kedua, cadangan saya bahawa pengasingan asrama untuk pelajar senior dan junior perlu dilakukan supaya tidak bercampur di luar bilik darjah. Tempat sembahyang, kantin, riadah dan tandas perlu diasingkan atau mengikut giliran supaya tiada percampuran senior dan junior langsung. Audit harus memastikan perkara paling penting ini.

Ketiga, cadangan saya supaya warden dan pengawal keselamatan meronda sekeliling sekolah dan asrama secara rambang sekurang-kurangnya tiga kali setiap hari, walaupun CCTV beroperasi. Imej pengawal meronda penting supaya pembuli tidak berani bertindak sewenang-wenangnya. Penggunaan dron sebagai kawalan tambahan boleh dijadikan amalan keselamatan.

Keempat, audit harus memastikan semua pintu bilik darjah, dewan atau makmal dan setor dikunci apabila tidak digunakan. Kematian pelajar Tingkatan 4, Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairoul Faisal di sebuah sekolah di Yong Peng, Johor mungkin dapat dihalang, jika pintu dewan dikunci, tetapi kini 'nasi sudah menjadi bubur'.

Kelima, semua guru sekolah harus mengikuti kursus mengenal pasti buli dalam kalangan pelajar serta membuat persediaan seperti kaedah menyoal pelajar, pemerhatian kelas serta penulisan laporan tindakan kepada guru disiplin. Guru yang sekolah asrama diaudit akan ditempatkan di sekolah berdekatan rumah mereka selepas kursus disempurnakan.

Keenam, audit juga perlu memastikan 'penalti' dikenakan terhadap kakitangan pentadbiran dan warden apabila kejadian buli mengakibatkan kecederaan serius serta kematian. Setakat ini, tidak kira berapa ramai pelajar yang mati atau cedera dibuli, kakitangan pentadbiran tetap dinaikkan pangkat dan gaji bertambah setiap tahun.

Akhir sekali, tiba masanya menyimpulkan kebenaran yang perit, penyeliaan sekolah berasrama gagal menjadi payung keselamatan dan kesihatan anak Melayu kita. Kita perlu menyifatkan masalah buli sebagai threat to nation dan mencari kaedah terbaik untuk menyelesaikannya.

38781b6b01f68521: A friend offered me a free ticket to the Bahrain Grand Prix at our very own Sepang International Circuit. I sadly declined. The crowd and the noise would have driven me crazy and it was best I stayed on my sofa watching the race on TV.
Here’s what I noticed afterwards: the single biggest type of comment on the many social media posts about it was: "Bring back F1 to Sepang!"

Malaysia hosted F1 races for 18 seasons until 2017. We watched Michael Schumacher, Lewis Hamilton, Sebastian Vettel, Fernando Alonso, etc., duke it out on one of the most beautiful motor racing circuits in the world. Then F1 went away.
It’s incredibly expensive to host F1 races with uncertain returns. At some point somebody did the numbers and pulled the plug. Sepang circuit went quiet, at least to Formula 1 races.

But its reputation remains. F1 aficionados looked forward to F1's return to Sepang. What I had thought were just irritations about Sepang, especially the afternoon rains, were actually what made races at Sepang unique, challenging and exciting.

Technically, the recent race was a Bahrain event hosted by Sepang after Bahrain cancelled their own event because of the war going on in that region. Their loss is our gain and now Bahrain as well as any of the other F1 hosts know that Sepang is always available to step in.

Being a last-minute host does bring about its share of problems. The crowd was huge – in excess of a quarter of a million people over the race weekend - and created massive issues with transport, safety, amenities, etc.

But such problems are unavoidable for such a late substitution, and they don’t detract from the race's success. That’s important because the race itself was amazing. The Sepang circuit lived up to its reputation, but other factors added to the drama.
The glitches in various software on the race cars as well as the rules around them caused by the rain will lead to major changes and Sepang will be remembered for that in F1 lore.

That so many people turned out over the long weekend surprised me. I had thought F1 had become passé and that the generation of us who like to hear cars that deafen us has been replaced by those who prefer the quiet swooshing of electric vehicles.

It seems the demise of petrol heads like us has been greatly exaggerated. There’s something captivating – perhaps a pleasure, perhaps a fear or perhaps both at once – in the ear-piercing shrieks of metal and rubber being propelled and piloted at ungodly speeds.

Not all of us old timers are old fossils whining about the demise of ICE (internal combustion engine) cars. The future is electric and F1 itself has been dipping its toes in it, even with the occasional hiccups we just saw.
Electric car racing will bring its own set of excitement when its time comes, and I'm sure Sepang will be ready for it.

For now, I’m happily basking in the reflected glory of Sepang’s success. Singapore’s own F1 race on its night-time street circuit is next, but I can guarantee that it’ll be judged less exciting than Sepang.

Singapore’s race is very much like Monaco’s – glitz, glamour and wealth with the vagaries of Sepang’s heat, humidity and rain added. It’s a finely-tuned race on streets that is not quite a free-for-all on a purpose-built circuit. There, you cannot hear the crowd’s roar over the cacophony when Lewis Hamilton brilliantly executes an overtaking manoeuvre.

At Sepang, Hamilton came third for a podium finish. Max Verstappen won this race, just as he won the very last race in Sepang in 2017. Fernando Alonso did well too. The old-timers are still around and kicking butt even in the much-maligned new F1 cars, rules, and technologies.

I’ve driven on the Sepang circuit in fancy German sports cars courtesy of another generosity. But high speeds freak me out and get my heart palpitating almost as fast as the engine’s revolutions. Brutal speed is not for me, and truth be told, I find rallying more exciting and freakish than F1.

But the world loves F1 more, and apparently loves Sepang very much too. Verstappen will certainly remember his victories here, especially his latest one. Sepang’s brilliant circuit plus the uncertainties of the weather – especially the heat and rain, and hopefully this time only, the haze – make it unique.

I wouldn’t be surprised if they bring F1 back to Sepang. If the economics work out, it would be an absolutely brilliant annual event for F1 lovers the world over and it’ll put Sepang closer to the rarified company of legendary F1 circuits past and present such as Monza, Silverstone, Spa-Francorchamps and Nürburgring.
I would be even less likely to attend, however, even if I were to become completely deaf, as my aversion to crowds wouldn’t change, and most likely would have increased.

But I’d enjoy it vicariously and derive great pleasure in hearing it described as one of the most exciting motor races in the F1 calendar, one held within a week of the race in Singapore where spectators and drivers go to relax and play go-karts over some streets for a few hours.

fc3b064dc8ef63ad: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The sudden announcement by local film distributor Antenna Entertainments that A24’s psychological thriller "Primetime" has been banned by the Film Censorship Board (LPF) is more than a disappointment for film fans and scholars alike.
As a critical media studies scholar analysing our regulatory systems, I see this as a glaring case of policy misalignment that actively undermines the government’s own economic directives.
Once again, a high-profile international asset has been flatly erased from the local market without public justification.
Instead of treating these adjustments as routine protection, the government must evaluate how opaque decisions create structural risks that dismantle the industry.
If we expect our creative sectors to thrive globally, we must stop allowing unpredictable censorship to disrupt them from within.
Destabilising the Finas growth mandate
This enforcement strategy directly contradicts the developmental goals of the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas).

Just recently, Finas chairman Hans Isaac made a strong public case for increased national budget allocations to strengthen the local film ecosystem and elevate the global competitiveness of Malaysian stories.
The complete ban on "Primetime" represents a stark policy paradox that terrifies investors.
Instead of building a viable market, heavy-handed bans signal to international studios that the Malaysian theatrical space is highly volatile.
This regulatory uncertainty creates a chilling effect, forcing local filmmakers into defensive self-censorship out of fear their projects will be permanently shelved.
If the government wants a return on investment for public funds, it must first guarantee a stable environment where creative risks can safely exist.
Loss of public pedagogy and revenue

From an educational and media literacy standpoint, erasing complex texts like "Primetime", which critiques vigilante media and the sensationalism surrounding child exploitation, is deeply counterproductive.
Banning a film does not stop it from being consumed in the digital age. A theatrical ban simply drives audiences to illicit online spaces and foreign streaming platforms.
Instead of protecting the public, the government achieves zero educational oversight while local exhibitors and cinemas lose vital box-office revenue.
We are effectively routing taxable domestic entertainment expenditure straight out of the country, starving the exact ecosystem the communications ministry is trying to fund.
If we want citizens to develop critical thinking skills, we cannot keep removing the very educational materials required to teach them.
Need for structural transparency
We must move beyond treating film as mere passive entertainment.
Finas CEO Azmir Saifuddin Mutalib recently said that the censorship framework has shown signs of opening up by increasingly relying on age classifications like PG-18 over extensive cuts.
The banning of "Primetime" feels like a massive step backward from that progressive rhetoric.
Instead of systemic censorship that suffocates open discussion, LPF must transition toward a transparent classification system.
The board must publicly publish detailed, analytical justifications for its restrictions.
Explaining why a piece of content crosses cultural boundaries helps educate the public on media ethics and artistic boundaries, fostering a mature and responsible film culture.
If we trust Malaysians to vote, pay taxes, and raise families, we should at least trust them to sit in a dark room and critically analyse a movie.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an associate professor in critical media studies at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia’s Centre for Research in Media and Communication and an FMT reader.

0c3a0aba01ce49de: We are told from childhood to heed traffic rules. Yet anyone who has driven on our roads knows that many of us treat them as suggestions, heeding them only when a policeman is visible at the junction. The moment we see that uniform, compliance becomes instantaneous.
We obey not because we have internalised the law’s moral force; we obey because we fear being caught.
This is not a peculiarity of Malaysian drivers — it is a reflection of human nature everywhere. And it applies just as much to the scourge of corruption.
People do not walk away from corrupt practices simply because they have learned to hate corruption or because it is a religious injunction. They stop because they fear being caught.
This observation exposes the limits of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s recent message to Gen Z.

Speaking at the National Student Figure Awards on Oct 1, 2026, he reminded undergraduates that a degree or a doctorate is no shield against greed. He noted that many of those implicated in major scandals such as 1MDB, Felda, and Tabung Haji are well educated.

His conclusion was sound: “A good education, therefore, does not make one virtuous.” But speeches are traffic signs — necessary, yet powerless without the policeman standing behind them. Advice, after all, is the easiest thing a politician can give.

Anwar also said he would be relentless in his pursuit of corrupt officials past and present, regardless of political fallout. Which means his rhetoric rests on two pillars: cultivating character in our young and pursuing corrupt officials.

Preaching to students costs nothing. It does not ask anyone in power to surrender their influence. Building a truly independent enforcement mechanism, however, is expensive, politically risky, and institutionally demanding.
Anwar should know this better than most. He spent decades on the outside arguing for these very structural changes. Now, he holds the keys to the house and he must build that policeman.

To be fair, the administration has taken formal steps, such as the establishment of the National Education Council and the National Education Blueprint 2026–2035, which aim to strengthen values and morals from primary school through higher learning.
This is a welcome bridge. But forming a council or launching a national plan is not the same as implementing deep reform.

Character education cannot remain trapped as slogans in civics textbooks. It requires teachers trained in moral reasoning rather than rote recitation; and it requires ethics to be treated with utmost seriousness in fields where misconduct carries the highest stakes — medicine, engineering, finance, and public administration.
Strengthening values in educational institutions will help the next generation and beyond. But a capable and independent policeman is needed at the junction today.

While the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) possesses the statutory power to initiate investigations independently, its structural vulnerability stems from executive oversight — chiefly that its leadership serves at the pleasure of the executive.

Reform advocates including G25 and Bersih have long urged that the MACC be removed from the Prime Minister’s Department and placed under parliamentary oversight via a constitutionally mandated independent anti-corruption commission.

But to be fair, the MACC under Anwar recorded 1,095 charges and 563 convictions from 2,633 investigation papers opened since 2024, with 583 involving high-profile and public-interest cases. Asset recovery has been aggressive: RM6.81 billion seized between January and August 2025 alone, against leakages estimated at RM277 billion over six years.
And three former prime ministers are among several top politicians facing trial.

Yet we see more cases of corruption emerging — Najib Razak’s discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) in his SRC International case (June 2025), ongoing probes into defence procurement and military officers, and Anwar’s public backing of MACC investigations into senior officials, the MACC 'corporate mafia' allegation — and we shake our heads saying corruption has become systemic.

Why? Is it that those handling public money are unafraid of being caught if they indulge in corruption? Is it because they feel they can get away if they are connected? Is it because givers feel they will get away with it? If this is so, enforcement needs to be tightened and those enforcing it must be of unquestionable integrity.

Do businessmen resort to bribes because they see it as the only way to ensure swift clearance of their problems or approvals for their initiatives by civil servants? If this is so, the systems and processes used by regulators need improvement.

Is corruption systemic because political parties are funded by monetary gifts from those who have gained government contracts? If so, the registrar of societies and the MACC need to scrutinise the accounts of all political parties to the minutest detail.

Also, there is the credibility question. Persistent structural bottlenecks — such as prosecutorial discretion resting solely with the attorney general — continue to fuel public perceptions of selective enforcement.

Hassan Abdul Karim, the admirable Pakatan Harapan MP for Pasir Gudang, told Parliament in January that government efforts were affected by public perception that corruption cases were being investigated inconsistently.
“From the outside, people see that some cases are investigated quickly, some are delayed, and sometimes cases are not investigated at all. Some cases lead to charges quickly, while others do not.”

Asking how the government could fully implement anti-corruption measures if elites and high-ranking national leaders received “discounts,” he said: “I am not saying this is a mistake, but something is not right. On one hand, we want to fight corruption fully, yet on the other, some are let off with ‘discounts’.”

“Moreover, among our elite leaders, both past and present, many court cases end with DNAA. Not only that, some are then given NFA (no further action). I sympathise with the officers of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission who diligently investigate these cases.”
No one can seriously argue against his points.

Civil society organisations such as Transparency International Malaysia have also reminded us that stagnant global perceptions reflect lingering anxieties over unresolved high-profile cases and controversial DNAA decisions.

Therefore, any move to make the MACC more effective and independent must be paired with the long-debated separation of powers between the attorney general (the government’s chief legal adviser) and the public prosecutor (who holds absolute constitutional discretion under Article 145(3) to institute, conduct, or discontinue criminal proceedings).
Although the government has agreed in principle to split these roles, the slow pace of constitutional amendments leaves a system where prosecutorial discretion remains tied to the executive.
This is the challenge facing the prime minister: he must willingly constrain his own power over the machinery of justice. And I don’t envy him.

As prime minister, Anwar holds the power to initiate and constitutionalise MACC independence, finalise the separation of the public prosecutor from the attorney general, reform public procurement and political financing, protect whistleblowers, ensure greater government transparency, and allow more freedom of expression.
Moral speeches set the tone; but the harder work is restructuring our systems so that corruption becomes difficult, risky, and socially unsustainable.
Our prime minister has told young Malaysians to hate corruption. He now has the historic opportunity to build the independent institutions that make wrongdoers fear it.

Just as we need the red lights and the visible policeman at the traffic junction to ensure full compliance, we need to complement advice and education in values with an effective and independent MACC and an autonomous prosecutor to put fear into potential wrongdoers and enforce the message that no one is above the law.
